questions.q: What does "self-similarity" mean in the context of fractals? Give one example from nature.
questions.a: Self-similarity means a shape looks similar to itself at different scales; a small part resembles the whole. Example: a fern frond — each leaflet looks like a miniature version of the whole frond. A wrong answer (e.g., "it means the shape is symmetric" or "it means the pattern repeats exactly like wallpaper") reveals confusion between symmetry/repetition and scale-invariant self-similarity.

questions.q: Why is the self-similarity of a coastline called "statistical" rather than "exact"? Explain using the idea of zooming in.
questions.a: Exact self-similarity means every small part is an identical copy of the whole (like in mathematical fractals). Coastlines have statistical self-similarity: the jaggedness at 1 km scale has the same statistical roughness as at 1 m scale, but the exact bays and peninsulas are not identical copies. A wrong answer (e.g., "because coastlines are not perfectly symmetric") shows the student hasn't grasped the distinction between exact geometric copying and statistical distribution of features across scales.

questions.q: A student draws a tree where the trunk splits into 3 branches, each of those splits into 3 smaller branches, and each of those splits into 3 twigs. At each level, the branching angle and relative length are the same. Is this tree exactly self-similar or statistically self-similar? Justify your answer.
questions.a: This tree is exactly self-similar because the branching rule (3 branches, same angle, same length ratio) is applied identically at every scale without randomness. In nature, trees have statistical self-similarity because branching angles and lengths vary randomly. A wrong answer (e.g., "statistical because it's a tree") indicates the student thinks all natural objects are automatically statistical, missing that the student's drawing is a deterministic mathematical model.

questions.q: Compare the self-similarity in a cauliflower and a river network (like the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta). How are they similar and how do they differ in terms of the branching process?
questions.a: Both show statistical self-similarity: cauliflower florets branch into smaller florets; river networks branch into tributaries. Similarity: both use repeated branching to fill space efficiently. Difference: cauliflower branching is driven by biological growth rules (cell division), while river branching is driven by erosion and water flow physics — the former is more regular, the more irregular. A weak answer (e.g., "both are fractals") without comparing the generative processes shows surface-level recognition without analytical depth.

questions.q: A classmate says: "A straight line is self-similar because if you zoom in, it still looks like a straight line. So a straight line is a fractal." Evaluate this statement and explain why it is correct or incorrect.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. While a straight line is exactly self-similar (any segment is a scaled copy of the whole), fractals are defined as shapes with detail at arbitrarily small scales and typically non-integer dimension. A straight line has no detail at any scale — it is smooth and has topological dimension 1, same as its fractal dimension. Fractals have fractal dimension > topological dimension. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "correct because it's self-similar") shows the student equates self-similarity alone with being a fractal, missing the requirement of complexity at all scales.

questions.q: Design a simple drawing rule (algorithm) that a Class 6 student could follow to create a statistically self-similar tree on paper. The rule must include randomness. Write the rule in 3-4 steps.
questions.a: Example rule: 1) Draw a vertical trunk of length 10 cm. 2) At the top, draw 2 or 3 branches (choose randomly) at angles between 20° and 50° from the trunk, each branch length = 0.6 × trunk length (multiply by a random factor between 0.5 and 0.7). 3) Repeat step 2 for each new branch, stopping when branch length < 1 cm. 4) Add small random wiggles to each segment. A poor answer (e.g., "draw a tree with branches") lacks algorithmic precision, randomness specification, or stopping condition — showing inability to translate the concept into a generative process.
